newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Telephone firms can salivate over new markets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Telephone firms can salivate over new markets.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
"What is the biggest machine in the world?".
According to Dataquest analyst John Dinsdale, the unlikely answer is: the world telephone network.

Call the question unfair or obscure, but however you define it, the world telecommunications market is a monster. And after more than 100 years of growth, the old giant is set to charge into the next century with a new zest for life.
In a presentation to a recent symposium, Dinsdale pointed out that in 1996 the world's telecommunications market was worth more than $800 billion in sales.
(Dataquest is a market research subsidiary of U.S. technology consultancy Gartner Group.)

Far from becoming a staid and saturated industry, growth is poised to accelerate, boosted by the need for new telephones in underdeveloped regions and new markets for services sold across the Internet, Dinsdale said.
"There is enormous potential for future market growth. Network development has hardly started in many developing economic regions," he said.
BT-MCI SHOWS THE INTERNET IS TELECOMS FUTURE

The $20 billion merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI of the U.S., announced early this month, reflects the coming scramble by the world's leading telephone companies to sell services across the Internet, the world wide network of computers, Gartner Group analysts Anne-Marie Roussel and Nigel Deighton told Reuters.
These companies need to operate globally to attack these new markets.

"We are looking at the death of the national player. We are looking at the globalisation of enterprises generally. German companies will have clients in the U.S. and France and the UK. Somebody who has only a national mindset is going to die in the long run and that is why we are looking at globalisation of services," Roussel said.
And the Internet is going to be a key vehicle for successful telephone companies.
"Definitely what is happening now is the Internet. Those who are late on picking up on this are going to be squashed," Roussel said.

"Certainly BT MCI are positioning themselves very strongly providing Internet services. The Internet is simply the best way to communicate with clients for big businesses like banks to other big businesses," she said.

According to Deighton, BT MCI, to be known as Concert Communications Services, will also see more aggressive action soon from other alliances like ATT and its World Partners grouping, and Global One International linking Sprint Corp of the U.S., Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom.

Deighton says MCI already provides around 40 per cent of U.S. Internet market backbone capacity -- the telephone lines and hardware which carries the Internet traffic -- and the newly merged company will extend that backbone to Europe and Asia.

"BT MCI seems to be one of the first organisations that have begun to realise how important this phenomonom will be. And in building this global internet backbone they are reserving capacity for corporate Intranet traffic," Deighton said.
Intranets are private, mostly corporate, secure networks of personal computers.

"We are seeing the beginnings of global carriers preparing to hijack the high-value business of the Internet and put it into electronic networks where they will be able to charge a premium," according to Deighton.
EMERGING MARKETS SHORT OF TELEPHONES
But it is not only these high-tech corporate markets that will light a fire under the telephone business.

"The telephone growth rate potential is enormous. Even in Europe there are countries which have below 40 lines per 100 population. You get into Africa and you get as low as two or three," Roussel said.
In the United States, the world's most saturated telephone market, there are 61 telephones per 100 population. In Western Europe the figure is 45, according to Dataquest.
And this is also good news for telephone equipment makers.
EQUIPMENT SUPPLIERS TO SHARE IN BONANZA
"In India, in China, in Africa there is an enormous potential for not only the BT MCIs, the carriers, but for people who sell equipment, who build those networks," Roussel said.
"We are going to see an enormous amount of business being done in those kinds of countries -- Alcatel, Siemens, Ericsson, Nokia, they are looking at those markets with big, huge eyes," Roussel said.
But there dangers as well as profits for operators in third world markets.

"Although these markets have huge potential, it is sometimes difficult to repatriate profits. It is not clear that they will represent the same degree of profitability that they have in Western markets," warned Deighton.
HUGE LONG-TERM GROWTH FOR TELEPHONE MARKETS
No doubt ambitious companies will listen to these cautionary words, but might pay more attention to Dataquest's Dinsdale.

"Newly privatised markets in western Europe will generate more than $30 billion from new operators in the next 10 years, and they will spend some $15 billion a year on telecommunications network systems," Dinsdale said.
"Telecommunications is one of the very few guaranteed long-term growth markets, and what has historically been a staid and static market is now changing dramatically."
